trace.claim: The paper asks whether hostile political expression on X/Twitter is associated with political engagement and its antecedents, beyond deprivation or personality-based explanations.

Online political hostility among American X/Twitter users is positively associated with indicators of political engagement and its antecedents, strongest for political interest, political knowledge and online participation.
The study combines two years of X behavioral data with panel survey data from American users.
The linked panel sample includes 2,567 users with survey responses matched to X handles.
Online political hostility is measured with a Super-Unsupervised word-embeddings approach averaging post-level similarity to a political hate vector.
Indicators of political engagement and its antecedents are positively associated with online political hostility.
The authors avoid claims about formal network influence or centrality.
The authors place the paper in a revisionist view of political engagement and extend it to online political hostility.
Classical research is cited as emphasizing that education, internal efficacy, political interest, political knowledge and participation are central to democratic engagement.
